newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's Bucaram defiant as pressure builds.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's Bucaram defiant as pressure builds.

text.p: Ecuador's Abdala Bucaram, defiant in the face of mounting pressure for his removal from the presidency, said on Saturday he would rather die than step down in disgrace.
"They want to get me out of the presidency. I swear on my children, on my family and on my country that I'd rather die than resign," he said.
Bucaram, who was voted out of office by Congress on grounds of mental incompetence on Thursday, has dismissed the move as a "coup" and insisted he has no plans to relinquish the reins of power.

But the man popularly known as "El Loco", or "madman", suffered another major setback in his fight for political survival on Saturday when his defence minister resigned citing the military's professed neutrality in the constitutional crisis over leadership.

The resignation of Gen. Victor Bayas followed that of three other cabinet officials in 48 hours, including Energy Minister Alfredo Adum, and left Bucaram looking very much alone at the top of his six-month-old government.
It also came amid unconfirmed reports on national radio that the military had withdrawn all support from Bucaram.
Bucaram left the heavily fortified presidential palace in Quito late on Friday for his traditional power base in Guayaquil.
His comment about preferring death to resignation came in a speech to supporters in a working-class district on the outskirts of the Pacific coast city.

In the same speech, in which he identified himself as "commander-in-chief of the poor," he said nothing would prevent him from finishing his full term of office, which ends in August 2000. Surprisingly, given intense political pressure for his removal from office, he also announced plans to run for re-election sometime after 2000.
Ecuador's Constitution bars anyone from serving two consecutive terms as president.

In a harangue later in central Guayaquil, Bucaram also called for a nationwide strike on Feb. 19 so that his supporters could protest against the "oligarchs" and "conspirators". He said they were responsible for the congressional vote to oust him.
"If the oligarchy wants war, it can have war," he said.
Ecuador was shut down by a nationwide strike on Wednesday and Thursday as the entire country rose up against tough economic measures the government unveiled in January.

Three top politicians, including Bucaram, have staked claims to the presidency since Thursday night. The other contenders are Vice President Rosalia Arteaga, who claims she is Bucaram's legal successor, and congressional leader Fabian Alarcon, who was named acting president by Congress.

Seeking to end the conflict, two former presidents endorsed calls on Saturday for the country's three current "presidents" to step aside in favour of a more neutral figure, to be selected by national consensus.
